objection: Does ‘firstborn of creation’ mean Jesus was created?
answer:
Peace to you as well, and thank you for asking so directly — this is precisely the right question to press, and I want to answer it on its own terms.

The Greek word Paul uses, prototokos, is fundamentally a title of rank and inheritance, not a marker of when someone came into existence. Scripture itself shows this: in Psalm 89:27 God says of David, "I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth" — yet David was neither God's literal son nor the first king of Israel. "Firstborn" there means supreme heir, preeminent one, not first-in-a-sequence.

But even setting the lexical point aside, look at what Paul himself does in the very next verse. Colossians 1:16 says "for by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible... all things were created by him, and for him." If the Son were himself one of the created things, Paul's sentence collapses into nonsense — the "firstborn of all creation" would be creating himself, and being included in the "all things" he creates. That is incoherent. Paul is not placing Christ first in the created order; he is placing him outside it, on the Creator's side of the Creator-creature line, with everything else — every throne, dominion, principality, power, visible and invisible — owing its existence to him.

This is confirmed by John 1:3: "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made." Not "almost all things," not "all things except himself" — all things, without remainder. If Christ made everything that was made, he was not himself made. So Colossians 1:15 doesn't contradict his eternity; rightly read in its own context, it establishes it. He is firstborn in the sense of supreme heir and sovereign head over creation, precisely because he is its uncreated source.
